planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this heirloom sport is maintained by division since spore-grown plants revert to plain fronds.

directions: Selected during the Victorian fern-collecting craze, this lady fern sport piles each frond tip and pinna tip into a dense cluster of forking, tassel-like crests rather than the plain taper of the wild species. The congested crests give the whole frond a bunched, corymb-like outline that holds its shape best in a sheltered spot out of drying wind. Grow in reliably moist, humus-rich woodland soil with the same part-to-full shade regime as common lady fern, and lift and divide crowded clumps every few years in spring since the crested habit can weaken vigor over time. Pair it with hostas or hardy geraniums where its ornate texture reads clearly against plainer foliage.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; like other named lady fern sports it must be propagated vegetatively to stay true to type.

directions: Another classic Victorian-era lady fern sport, this selection ends each pinnule lobe in a fine, bristle-like point, giving the twice-cut deciduous fronds a slightly spiky, textured edge that distinguishes it at a glance from smooth-margined forms. The arching habit and bright green spring fiddleheads are otherwise typical of the species, making it an easy substitute anywhere plain lady fern would be used. Keep soil consistently moist and rich in organic matter through the growing season, and expect fronds to collapse cleanly after the first hard frost before re-emerging in spring. Divide congested multi-crown clumps in early spring if frond quality declines.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this delicate heirloom clone is slower and less vigorous than the species and the later 'Clarissima Jones' selection, so give it an undisturbed spot.

directions: Known to Victorian fern collectors as the Kalon fern, this is among the most finely dissected of all hardy lady fern sports, with each frond cut and re-cut into a lacy, almost feathery texture that reads as a soft green haze rather than distinct pinnae. It is notably more delicate and slower to bulk up than either the plain species or the later, more robust 'Clarissima Jones' selection, so avoid dense competition from neighboring perennials. Grow in sheltered, evenly moist shade with rich organic soil, and mulch lightly over winter in colder zones to protect the crown. Divide only when strictly necessary, since this cultivar resents disturbance more than most lady fern forms.

planting.note: Divide established crowns or plant nursery divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a named clonal selection kept true to type by division.

directions: This dwarf, densely crested selection of the golden-scaled male fern packs its pinnae and frond tips into tight, bunched crests, giving a much more compact, congested silhouette than the taller crested forms like 'Cristata' or 'Cristata Angustata'. Emerging croziers still show the warm rust-orange scaling typical of the species, but the whole plant stays low and dense enough to use as a structural edge along a shaded path rather than a specimen clump. It shares the species' tolerance of drier shade once established and remains substantially evergreen through mild winters. Lift and divide multi-crowned clumps in early spring only when the center becomes congested and frond quality starts to decline.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring into humus-rich, constantly moist soil in partial to full shade; this New Zealand native is more cold-sensitive than many hardy ferns, so protect it where winters drop much below the mid-teens Fahrenheit.

directions: Native to forest understories, stream banks, and shaded rock faces across New Zealand, this small evergreen fern forms a neat clump of narrow, once-pinnate fronds with lance-shaped leaflets, a simpler and finer-textured look than the broad, leathery fronds of many other cultivated Blechnum species. It is closely related to and sometimes confused with its NZ cousins in mixed native plantings, occasionally hybridizing where ranges overlap. Give it a permanently damp, shaded site such as a streamside bed or fernery, since it has little tolerance for either direct sun or drying out between waterings. In marginal zones, grow it in a container that can be moved under cover for winter rather than risking it in open ground.
